cards.front: Recall a key point about Price Determination
cards.back: Equilibrium price is where supply equals demand — the market clears with no excess.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Price Determination
cards.back: Excess demand (shortage) occurs below equilibrium — consumers want more than producers supply, pushing price up. Excess supply (surplus) above equilibrium pushes price down.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Price Determination
cards.back: An increase in demand raises equilibrium price and quantity. An increase in supply raises quantity but lowers price.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Price Determination
cards.back: When both supply and demand shift, the effect on price or quantity depends on relative size of shifts.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Price Determination
cards.back: Revenue = price x quantity. On a diagram, revenue is the rectangle formed by equilibrium price and quantity. Price rises don't always increase revenue — depends on PED.

cards.front: What should you know about economics exam tips?
cards.back: When analysing price changes, use the DEM framework: Direction (which way do curves shift?), Extent (how large, depends on elasticity?), Magnitude of effect (what happens to P and Q?).

cards.front: What does Qd vs Qs mean?
cards.back: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (e.g. Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded)
Upward (prices tend to rise) (e.g. Downward (prices tend to fall))
Consumers bid up prices; producers supply more (e.g. Firms cut prices to sell stock; consumers buy more)
Pandemic toilet paper shortage 2020 (e.g. Excess high-street retail stock in recessions)
May impose price cap or rationing (e.g. May buy surplus or subsidise demand)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: If supply increases, producers always benefit because they sell more. Correct: While supply increases mean more quantity sold, the price falls. Whether producers benefit depends on elasticity: if demand is elastic, revenue rises.
